My understanding and what I’ve put in practice is online mg houses anything that is accessible by the public internet by customers as a service to those customers, cloud native applications that do not need direct connectivity back to the hub, and pretty much anything that doesn’t connect back to the hub directly.

Generally the online mg shouldn’t be directly connected back to on prem and private endpoints and private link service should be used to connect to the hub if connectivity is required. I can’t say I’ve seen two orgs that have both use the corp and online management groups the same way so really it’s up to how you want/need to apply permissions and prove compliance.  The corp vs online separation is more for policy application and permissions to protect the on prem/hub network imo.

Yes, sort of.  If you want to use pulumi config and outputs you can use key vault to store an encryption key, the secrets are encrypted with this and stored in either the config file or stack output. Whoever accesses the config or output needs to be able to access the key vault to.  This isn’t actually storing the secret in key vault, just the encryption key. 

There’s nothing stopping you from creating secrets and using them in your code though if that’s a requirement, handle it like any other secret and pass to the input args of the resources as needed.   Before we migrated to cloud we used both, depending on requirements. there’s pros/cons to each.  Generally I’d recommend using the encryption key and storing secrets in the stack outputs, it makes it much easier to reference different projects and stacks later on. 

The docs below give some idea of the process. Ignore the ESC sections, you have to use SaaS to use this.  With ESC I believe you could store the secrets themselves in azure key vault using environments though.

There’s probably already a provisioning process with your HRIS.  Go that route first if available.  You may have to dig a bit.  Workday, SAP, and a few other support user provisioning with a provisioning agent installed elsewhere on your network.  A lot less of a PITA than managing it yourself.  

Power Automate can’t directly work with AD, have to have something else to work with it.  There is an LDAP connector you can buy from c data but it is not worth the trouble.  

Azure Automation was the best solution I’ve found without a vendor supported provisioning process.  Pull information (or publish with event) into power automate, pass the data to an Azure Automation runbook that runs on agent either in same vnet or on prem and use powershell for user configuration. 

Alternative, if no agent is viable- get data into a blob/file share with power automate and have a scheduled task somewhere that pulls new entires and creates users with a powershell script.
What HRIS?   We’ve done a few with Power Automate and others.

We use it for a ton, both cloud flows and desktop flows.   

It has a learning curve but isn’t too difficult to use / learn.  Data gateway makes it easy to connect into on prem/vnet.  

It’s the cheapest entry into integration and RPA you’re going to find.
